div.p: The efficacy of radiotherapy for brain tumors is limited by tumor cell radio-resistance and the immunosuppressive microenvironment, which often counteracts the immunogenic effects of radiation-induced antitumor responses.

To address this, we developed statherin-enriched engineered outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), co-labeled with the radionuclide 131 I and loaded with the metabolic inhibitor methotrexate (MTX), termed 131 I-O/M-P, to enable integrated radiotoxicity, metabolic intervention, and immune activation. Upon delivery of 131 I-O/M-P to the tumor site, 131 I promptly emits β-rays that induce DNA double-strand breaks, triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD) and the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby initiating antitumor immune responses. Subsequently, the released MTX is internalized by tumor cells, where it inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocks nucleotide synthesis, impairs DNA repair capacity, and exacerbates DNA damage accumulation, thereby further promoting apoptosis and immune activation. Meanwhile, the intrinsic adjuvant properties of OMVs synergize with the ICD response to enhance T cell activation and infiltration. In both subcutaneous and orthotopic brain tumor mouse models, 131 I-O/M-P significantly enhanced CD8 + T cell infiltration, reduced T cell exhaustion phenotypes, and suppressed tumor growth. In summary, we present a temporally coordinated radio-metabolicimmunotherapy strategy, offering a novel therapeutic approach for advancing radio-immunotherapy in brain tumors.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Gliomas, particularly malignant brain tumors, represent one of the most aggressive and therapeutically challenging malignancies of the central nervous system [1][2][3].

eir complex genetic heterogeneity, deep infiltrative growth, and strong immune evasion characteristics severely limit the long-term efficacy of current treatment strategies [4][5][6][7]. Radiotherapy remains a key standard treatment modality for brain tumors and is widely employed as an adjuvant therapy after surgical resection and for controlling tumor recurrence [8][9][10][11]. However, clinical observations and preclinical studies have demonstrated that radiotherapy alone often yields limited efficacy due to the intrinsic radio-resistance of tumor cells and the presence of an immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) [12][13][14]. Glioma cells can resist radiation-induced damage by modulating the cell cycle to avoid radiosensitive phases, enhancing DNA repair capacity, and activating immunosuppressive pathways, such as the recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and M2-polarized macrophages, ultimately leading to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence [15][16][17][18]. erefore, simultaneously overcoming tumor cell radio-resistance and effectively activating antitumor immune responses during brain tumor radiotherapy is of great significance for improving therapeutic response, delaying tumor progression, and enhancing patient prognosis.

Methotrexate (MTX), a classical folate metabolism antagonist, inhibits key metabolic enzymes such as dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), thereby blocking nucleotide synthesis, limiting DNA repair, and inducing cell apoptosis [19][20][21]. e S-phase-specific activity of MTX makes it an ideal radio-sensitizer [22][23][24]. However, the clinical efficacy of MTX remains unsatisfactory, mainly due to the lack of effective tumor-targeted delivery systems and coordinated control mechanisms, which limits its potential in radio-sensitization and immune modulation [25,26]. erefore, it is urgent to develop a strategy that enables spatiotemporally coordinated delivery of radiotherapy and metabolic intervention within the tumor site to enhance treatment precision and efficacy.

On the other hand, radiotherapy can induce ICD, leading to the release of various damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), such as HMGB1, calreticulin (CRT), and ATP, which activate dendritic cells (DCs) and promote T cell mediated immune responses [27][28][29][30]. However, the TIME in brain tumors is characterized by an abundance of MDSCs, exhausted T cells, and high expression of immune checkpoint molecules [31][32][33][34].

ese factors markedly suppress the immune responses triggered by ICD, resulting in limited and short-lived immune activation [35][36][37]. erefore, amplifying ICD signals and synergizing them with sustained adjuvant immune stimulation may overcome the current limitations of radiotherapy-induced immune activation, thereby establishing a more durable and effective systemic antitumor immune response [38,39].

In recent years, engineered outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) have attracted increasing attention in cancer therapy due to their excellent biocompatibility, intrinsic immunogenicity, and versatile engineering and modification capabilities [40][41][42][43]. OMVs are derived from Gram-negative bacteria and are naturally enriched with pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and peptidoglycans [44][45][46].

ese components endow OMVs with intrinsic adjuvant properties, enabling them to efficiently promote DCs maturation and enhance CD8 + T cells activation, thereby boosting antitumor immune responses [47][48][49]. Meanwhile, their stable lipid bilayer structure allows for the encapsulation of various functional molecules, such as small-molecule drugs, nucleic acids, and radionuclides, providing excellent delivery capability [50][51][52]. Especially after genetic engineering or physicochemical modification, OMVs can further enhance their drug-loading

div.p: efficiency, targeting capability, and controlled functional release, making them an ideal platform for constructing multifunctional tumor therapy systems [53][54][55][56].

erefore, constructing a synergistic therapeutic system based on engineered OMVs that can simultaneously deliver radioactive isotopes (such as 131 I) and metabolic inhibitors while retaining intrinsic immune-adjuvant properties holds great promise. is strategy not only integrates radiotoxicity, metabolic intervention, and immune activation into a unified platform, but also enables spatially precise targeting and temporally sequential release. Such a system may overcome the limitations of conventional therapies in delivery efficiency and immune activation, offering a novel and comprehensive approach for the treatment of brain tumors.

Based on this, we constructed a multifunctional nanoplatform ( 131 I-O/M-P) by engineering OMVs expressing statherin-rich membrane proteins to co-deliver the radioactive isotope 131 I and the metabolic inhibitor MTX.

is platform achieves radio-metabolic-immunotherapeutic synergy through a triple mechanism: First, 131 I releases β-rays to induce DNA double-strand breaks in the tumor site, triggering ICD and the subsequent release of DAMPs; e subsequently released MTX can be taken up by tumor cells, where it inhibits DHFR activity, blocks nucleotide synthesis, arrests cell cycle progression, and limits DNA repair capacity, thereby exacerbating radiation-induced DNA damage and further promoting apoptosis; Meanwhile, OMVs possess intrinsic immuneadjuvant properties that enhance ICD signaling, promote DCs maturation and CD8 + T cell infiltration, and effectively alleviate T cell exhaustion. In addition, OMVs, together with radiation-induced DNA damage, synergistically activate the cGAS-STING signaling pathway, enhance NK cell activity, and markedly boost systemic antitumor immune responses. In both subcutaneous and orthotopic glioma models, 131 I-O/M-P exhibited potent antitumor efficacy by not only suppressing local tumor growth but also effectively reducing tumor invasiveness.

is therapeutic effect was accompanied by enhanced CD8 + T cell infiltration and alleviation of T cell exhaustion, validating the feasibility and translational potential of this multi-mechanism synergistic strategy in vivo. In summary, this study proposes a radio-metabolic-immunotherapeutic strategy centered on engineered OMVs, offering a novel and efficient integrated platform for glioma treatment. It also provides a theoretical foundation and technical support for the design of multi-mechanism-coupled tumor therapeutic systems.

div.head: Materials
div.p: VNP20009 was a kind gift from Prof Yang (Soochow University, China). Methotrexate (MTX) (Cat# M8971-5 g) and Isopropyl-β-D-iogalactoside (IPTG) (Cat# II0130-5 g) were purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Kanamycin (Cat# K331597-5 g) was procured from Aladdin. BCA Protein Assay Kit (Cat# P0012), 3,3'-dioctadecyloxacarbocyanine perchlorate (DiI) (Cat# C1036), Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK8) (Cat# C0038), Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Cat# C1062S) and DNA Damage Assay Kit by γ-H2AX Immunofluorescence (Cat# C2037S) were obtained from Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Na 125 I and Na 131 I solutions were procured from Shanghai Xinke Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Penicillin-streptomycin and cell culture medium were procured from Shanghai BasalMedia Technologies Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from Gibco. e antibodies used in this study was shown in Supplementary Table 1. All other reagents were acquired from local suppliers and used without further purifcation.

Five-week-old female C57BL/6J mice were purchased from the Experimental Animal Centre of Soochow University (Jiangsu, China), and all animal experiments were approved by the Animal Protection Committee of Soochow University (Jiangsu, China).

div.head: Preparation and characterization of OMVs, O/M and O/M-P
div.p: A modified pET28a expression vector carrying the AIDA-I auto-transporter domain and statherin (STATH) sequences was constructed and electro-transformed into the attenuated strain VNP20009.

OMVs were extracted from the STATH-VNP20009 using the ultracentrifugation method. Briefly, STATH-VNP20009 was inoculated into sterilized LB broth to the OD 600 = 0.6-0.8. Subsequently, 0.5 mM IPTG was added and the incubation was continued at 16 ℃ for 14 h to induce the expression of STATH. At the end of induction, the bacterium were removed by centrifugation at 4000 × g for 10 min and the supernatant was subsequently filtered using 0.22 μm filters. e supernatant was further concentrated using 100 kDa ultrafiltration tubes (Millipore), and then centrifuged at 150,000 × g for 2 h at 4 °C to obtain OMVs. e expression of STATH was verified by Western blot. For MTX loading, MTX and OMVs were mixed in different ratios and loaded with sonication. For the sonication method, the mixture was sonicated using a JY92-IIN Sonic Dismembrator (Tuohe, China) with the following settings: 20% amplitude, 3 s on/off for 10 min. In order to make the OMVs membrane recovery, the mixture was incubated at 37 ℃ for 2 h. Excess free MTX was removed using a 100 kDa ultrafiltration tube, and the amount of MTX loaded was quantified by UV-Vis spectrophotometry. e drug loading capacity (LC%) was calculated according to the following equation:
div.formula: LC (%) = Weight of MTX incorporated Weight of OMVs × 100%
div.p: MTX@OMVs-PEG (O/M-P) was produced through mixing MTX@OMVs (O/M) with DSPE-PEG 2000 , sonicating the mixture for 30 min, and then stirring it overnight. ey were quantified by a BCA protein assay and characterized by TEM and DLS. en 100 µg Na 2 S 2 O 5 was added to terminate the reaction and the reaction liquid was purified using ultrafiltration. e radio-labelling yield and stability were measured by paper chromatography method (PC). Whatman 3 mm chromatography paper was used as stationary phases and saline as the mobile phase. e stability of 125 I-O-P or 125 I-O/M-P (n = 3) in 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and PBS within 72 h was measured by this method.

div.head: In vitro cytotoxicity assay
div.p: To evaluate the in vitro biosafety of OMVs, HUVEC and GL261 cells were inoculated in a 96-well plate with 6 × 10 3 cells/well and incubated overnight. After removing the medium, different concentrations of OMVs (0, 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10, 20 µg/mL) were added for another 72 h incubation. en, the cells were treated with 100 µL of 10% CCK8 for 30 min.

e absorbance at 450 nm was measured by a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). For the cytotoxicity of MTX, GL261 cells were incubated with different concentrations of MTX (0, 0.098, 0.195, 0.391, 0.781, 1.563, 3.125, 6.25, 12.5, 25, 50 µg/mL) for 24 h. Similarly, to assess 131 I-O/M-P's cytotoxicity, GL261 cells were exposed to 10 µg/mL O/M-P, 3.7 MBq/mL 131 I, 3.7 MBq /mL 131 I-O-P, and 3.7 MBq /mL 131 I-O/M-P for 24 h.

div.head: Cellular uptake assay
div.p: GL261 cells (2 × 10 5 cells/well) were seeded in 12-well plates overnight. en, the cells were incubated with DiIlabelled O/M-P (10 µg/mL) for different time points (0, 1, 6 and 12 h). After treatments, the cells were collected for flow cytometry. Cellular uptake was further observed through confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM).

div.head: Cell cycle assays
div.p: For cell cycle analysis, GL261 cells (1 × 10 5 cells/dish) were seeded in 60 mm dishes overnight and then treated with MTX and O/M-P. After 24 h. cells were collected and fixed with precooled 70% ethanol at 4 °C overnight. Fixed cells were washed with PBS, stained with PI, and analyzed by flow cytometry. Cell cycle phases were quantified using FlowJo v10.

div.head: DNA damage assays
div.p: DNA damage assay Kit by γ-H2AX immunofluorescence was used to detect the extent of DNA damage of GL261 cells. Briefly, the GL261 cells (5 × 10 3 cells/dish) were seeded in confocal dishes and incubated with O/M-P, 131 I, 131 I-O-P, and 131 I-O/M-P for 24 h. After treatment, cells were immediately fixed and then stained with the γ-H2AX monoclonal antibody and DAPI. e extent of DNA damage was observed using the CLSM.

div.head: Western blotting
div.p: To analyze the effect of O/M-P on cyclin, GL261 cells were treated with MTX and O/M-P for 24 h. After treatment, total proteins were extracted with RIPA lysate and quantified using a BCA protein assay kit. SDS-PAGE was used to separate the protein samples from each group, which was then transferred to PVDF membranes. e PVDF membrane was incubated with primary antibodies cyclin A2 Polyclonal antibody, Proteintech; PCNA Polyclonal antibody, Proteintech) overnight at 4 ℃. Subsequently, the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies. Protein expression was evaluated by grayscale analysis. Meanwhile, the expression of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) was also analyzed by Western blot. Furthermore, western blotting was used to analyze the effect of 131 I-O/M-P on the expression of proteins related to the cGAS-STING pathway, such as p-STING and p-IRF3.

div.head: Cell apoptosis assay
div.p: Annexin V-FITC/PI apoptosis detection kit was used to detect the apoptosis rate of GL261 cells. GL261 cells (4 × 10 5 cells/well) were seeded in 6-well plates and incubated with O/M-P, 131 I, 131 I-O-P, and 131 I-O/M-P. After 24 h, cells were collected and stained for detection.

div.head: SPECT/CT imaging and bio-distribution of 125 I-O/M-P
div.p: To construct glioma subcutaneous tumors, 5-weekold C57BL/6 mice had their right axilla subcutaneously injected with 5 × 10 6 GL261-Luc cells suspended in 100 µL PBS. For orthotopic GBM tumors, C57BL/6 mice were anesthetized and fixed to the brain stereotaxic apparatus.

e scalp was sterilized and cut with a scalpel to expose the bregma. Holes were drilled using a small animal skull drill at the injection site (0.5 mm behind the coronal suture and 2.0 mm to the right of the sagittal suture). e micro-syringe slowly entered 3.5 mm deep and withdrew 0.5 mm. en, 10 µL of 1 × 10 6 GL261-Luc cell suspension was slowly injected at an injection rate of 1 µL/min. Following the injection, the injection was left for 5 min, and then the needle was slowly withdrawn and the skin of the mouse head was sutured. After the tumor model was successfully constructed, 125 I-O/M-P was injected into mice (subcutaneous tumor: intravenous injection (i.v.), 3.7 MBq of 125 I, 10 µg of OMVs; orthotopic tumor: intracranial injection, 1.85 MBq of 125 I, 5 µg of OMVs), followed by SPECT/CT imaging (MILabs, Netherlands; scan protocols: CT > SPECT; CT parameters: scan mode "fast", scan angle "full", scan time "3 min 24 sec; SPECT parameters: number of time frame "1", time per frame "10 min"), bio-distribution, and biosafety studies. SPECT/CT imaging and biodistribution studies were conducted at the specified time after injection to track the distribution of 125 I-O/M-P in different tissues and organs. For biodistribution studies, organs were collected, weighed and their radioactivity was measured with a gamma counter, with quantitative data expressed as % ID/g. Furthermore, 125 I-O/M-P's in vivo biosafety was assessed following a period of its administration. Before the experiment, the thyroid was blocked with 1% potassium iodide (KI).

div.head: Anti-tumor efficacy in subcutaneous glioma model
div.p: In order to evaluate the anti-tumor effect of 131 e body weight and tumor volume were recorded throughout the treatment period. e volume of the tumor was quantified using this formula: volume = (length) × (width) 2 /2. After treatment, tumor tissues and vital organs were removed for further experimental studies.

div.head: Anti-tumor efficacy in orthotopic implantation glioma model
div.p: As for orthotopic gliomas, they were randomly divided into 3 groups (n = 6): Ctrl (PBS), 131 I-O-P (1.85 MBq of 131 I, 5 µg of OMVs) and 131 I-O/M-P (1.85 MBq of 131 I, 5 µg of OMVs). e drugs were injected into the tumor via a brain stereotactic injection technique. After treatment, the mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and then intraperitoneally injected with 100 µL 5 mg/mL D-Luciferin sodium salt, and bioluminescence imaging (BLI) of the tumors was performed with the IVIS Lumina III imaging system (PerkinElmer, USA; scan protocols: luminescent, exposure time "30 s"). Subsequently, BLI was performed every 5 days to monitor tumors growth. Meanwhile, the body weight of mice was recorded throughout the treatment period. At the end of treatment, the mice were sacrificed, and brains and other major organs were removed for further study.

div.head: In vivo antitumor immune activation
div.p: After successful establishment of GL261-Luc subcutaneous and orthotopic glioma models, randomized grouping and treatment were performed. Five days after subcutaneous and orthotopic glioma treatment, tumors or ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes were removed. Single cell suspensions were then made according to with standard procedures. e cells from the lymph nodes were stained with anti-CD11c-FITC, anti-CD86-PE, and anti-CD80-APC for the DCs maturation study. For macrophage cells analyze, single-cell suspension was stained with anti-F4/80-FITC, anti-CD11b-Percp/Cy5.5, anti-CD86-PE and anti-CD86-APC for flow cytometry assay. For the evaluation of T cell and NK cell infiltration in tumor, single-cell suspension was stained with anti-CD3-FITC, anti-CD8a-PE, anti-Granzyme B-APC, anti-CD8a-PEcy7, anti-PD-1-PE, anti-CD45-PEcy7 and anti-NK1.1-PE antibodies.

div.head: Immunofluorescence staining
div.p: Tumor tissues from mice treated as described were fixed, followed by cryo-sectioning. e tissue sections were then stained with antibodies such as anti-γ-H2AX, antip-STING, anti-HMGB1, anti-CRT, and anti-HSP70 etc., employing either single or double staining techniques. Immunofluorescence images were acquired using a confocal microscope (FV1200, Olympus).

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: All experiment's results were presented as the mean ± SD. Statistical differences of multiple groups were calculated by Unpaired Student's t test using GraphPad Prism 9.5 (GraphPad Software, CA) software.

div.head: Construction and characterization of 131 I-O/M-P
div.p: e therapeutic efficacy of radiotherapy for brain tumors is limited by the intrinsic radio-resistance of tumor cells and the immune-suppressive microenvironment in which they reside; this dual barrier not only weakens the direct tumor-killing capacity of radiotherapy but also restricts the immune responses induced by irradiation. erefore, it is of great significance to develop an integrated therapeutic platform that can simultaneously enhance radiosensitivity and activate immune responses. In this study, we designed and constructed a multifunctional nanoplatform ( 131 I-O/M-P) that integrates radiation-induced damage, metabolic intervention, and immune activation, whose core structure comprises engineered OMVs co-loaded with the radionuclide 131 I and the metabolic inhibitor methotrexate (MTX) (Fig. 1A).

First, the tyrosine-and proline-rich salivary acidic protein statherin (STATH) was integrated into the outer membrane of the attenuated Salmonella typhimurium strain VNP20009 by genetic engineering (Fig. S1). STATH-OMVs were harvested by ultracentrifugation, and the successful display of STATH on the vesicle surface was verified by western blot (Fig. 1B). Subsequently, MTX was efficiently loaded into the interior of STATH-OMVs by probe sonication to form MTX@ OMVs (O/M) (Fig. 1C).

e results showed that the drug-loading efficiency was positively correlated with the mass ratio of MTX to OMVs. At a mass ratio of 10:1 (MTX: OMVs), the drug loading capacity (LC %) could stably reach above 28% (Fig. 1D). It may be possible to further improve drug loading capacity by means such as changing the loading method (e.g. endogenous drug loading). Considering the in vivo requirements for blood circulation time and immune-compatibility, we further modified the surface of O/M with DSPE-PEG 2000 to obtain PEGylated vesicles (O/M-P). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed a well-defined, typical vesicular morphology, with an average diameter of 85.55 nm and a zeta potential of -22.97 mV (Fig. 1E-G), indicating successful PEGylation without disrupting the vesicle structure. Meanwhile, DLS and Zeta potential measurements showed that MTX loading slightly increased the average hydrodynamic diameter of OMVs; the resulting O/M-P displayed a size of ~ 80 nm (consistent in magnitude with the TEM observation), and the zeta potential changed from -20.87 mV to -18.33 mV (Fig. 1F-G), suggesting that MTX encapsulation did not markedly affect the particle size or surface charge characteristics of OMVs.

Given that STATH displayed on the OMV surface contains multiple tyrosine residues, these aromatic sites can serve as high-density reactive sites for electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) of radioiodine ( 131 I/ 125 I), thereby markedly enhancing the efficiency of covalent labeling.

e resulting aryl C-I bond (iodinated tyrosine) exhibits high stability, which reduces in vivo de-iodination, enhances radio-chemical stability, and stably anchors the radionuclide on the vesicle surface; in the final 131 I-labeling system, this anchoring enables sustained local β-particle emission to exert radio-therapeutic effects. On this basis, we further carried out radio-iodination and stability assessments of O/M-P. For radiation safety and method optimization, and given the identical chemistry of 131 I and 125 I, we first employed the low-energy photon emitter 125 I (which decays predominantly by electron capture, accompanied by ~ 35 keV photons) to optimize conditions. Using the chloramine-T oxidation method, the labeling yields for O-P and O/M-P were 73.88 ± 4.07% and 74.52 ± 3.32%, respectively (Fig. 1H and Table S2), indicating high radio-labeling efficiency. Stability studies showed that the radio-chemical purity of 125 I-O/M-P remained above 80% after 72 h of incubation in PBS and 10% FBS (Fig. 1I), suggesting good in vitro radio-chemical stability under physiological-like conditions.

To conclude, we developed a multifunctional nanoplatform leveraging STATH-engineered OMVs, which exhibits robust radioiodine labeling capability, high MTX loading efficiency, and stable physicochemical properties and biocompatibility, thereby providing a solid carrier foundation for subsequent synergistic therapy that achieves tumor-cell metabolic interference, radio-sensitization, and immune activation.

div.head: I-O/M-P inhibits tumor cell-cycle and metabolism to enhance radio-sensitivity
div.p: After completing the physicochemical characterization of O/M-P, we next systematically validated its metabolicinterference and radio-sensitizing effects at the cellular level. First, CCK-8 assays showed that even at an OMV concentration of 20 µg/mL, the viability of HUVEC and GL261 cells exhibited no significant change (Fig. 2A), indicating good cytocompatibility of the carrier. Under the same conditions, we further evaluated the cytotoxicity of MTX and obtained an IC 50 of 2.070 µg/mL (4.555 µM) (Fig. S2), which informed subsequent dose selection for O/M-P.

ereafter, to confirm the prerequisite of cellular delivery, we examined the uptake of O/M-P. Flow cytometry and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) both showed time-dependent increases in O/M-P internalization by GL261 cells (Fig. 2B-D), indicating efficient entry into tumor cells, with uptake approaching saturation at approximately 6 h. is establishes the basis for O/M-P's intracellular actions.

After confirming that O/M-P can enter cells, we further examined whether it induces metabolic interference and cell-cycle alterations. Flow cytometry revealed that O/M-P increased the proportion of cells arrested in G1 (57.80 ± 1.42%) while decreasing the S-phase fraction (29.20 ± 0.87%) (Fig. 2E, F), indicating suppression of the G1/S transition and limitation of DNA synthesis. Consistently, western blotting showed downregulation of the cell-cycle/replication-associated proteins Cyclin A2 and PCNA (Fig. 2G, H); PCNA functions as the sliding clamp required for DNA replication and for gap-filling steps in several repair pathways (e.g., BER/NER), and its reduction is consistent with decreased DNA synthesis and impeded replication-fork progression. At the metabolic level, O/M-P decreased DHFR protein levels (Fig. 2I, J), consistent with inhibition of the folate cycle, and is inferred to impose nucleotide supply constraints and replication-associated stress. is inference aligns with the observed G1/S arrest and the downregulation of Cyclin A2 and PCNA (Fig. 2E-H), supporting an overall reduction in DNA replication and repair capacity. Accordingly, through the dual actions of perturbing tumor cell-cycle After confirming that O/M-P exerts metabolic interference in tumor cells, we further evaluated its radiosensitizing effect at the cellular level. On the basis of O/M-P-mediated suppression of replication-and repair-related processes, we accordingly constructed 131 I-O/M-P for tumor therapy and carried out mechanistic and functional validations. First, western blotting showed that p-STING and its downstream p-IRF3 were markedly increased after 131 I-O/M-P treatment (Fig. 2K, L). In light of the ionizing-radiation characteristics of 131 I, this finding suggests that radiation-induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and the consequent generation of cytosolic dsDNA fragments/micronuclei can be sensed by cGAS, thereby activating the cGAS-STING pathway; this, in turn, provides a molecular basis for enhanced antigen presentation in vivo, DCs maturation, and T/NKcell infiltration, establishing a potential immune coupling with radiotherapy. Regarding overall cytotoxic effects, CCK-8 assays showed that, compared with O/M-P or 131 I-O-P, 131 I-O/M-P further increased the inhibition rate against GL261 cells to 76.38 ± 2.50% (Fig. 2M), consistent with the signaling changes described above γ-H2AX immunofluorescence indicated that 131 I-O/M-P induced the most pronounced DNA damage (Fig. 2N, O). Mechanistically, the β -emissions from 131 I directly generate DSBs; in parallel, MTX-mediated DHFR inhibition, together with the observed downregulation of cell-cycle/ replication markers (Cyclin A2 and PCNA), suggests constraints on nucleotide supply and replication-related processes, thereby attenuating sublethal and potentially lethal damage repair (SLDR/PLDR) as well as repair pathways that depend on synthesis steps (e.g., the DNAsynthesis phases of HR and the gap-filling steps of SSBR).

is establishes synergy at the levels of increased damage and suppressed repair, ultimately enhancing radiosensitivity. To align molecular events with functional endpoints, we further assessed apoptosis. Annexin V/PI staining showed that 131 I-O/M-P significantly increased the apoptotic fraction of GL261 cells to 15.27 ± 3.28% (Fig. 2P, Q), providing a terminal phenotypic readout consistent with cell death driven by amplified radiation damage and constrained repair capacity. Moreover, the cell cloning results further confirmed the inhibitory effect of 131 I-O/M-P on GL261 cells (Figure S3). erefore, at the cellular level, 131 I-O/M-P orchestrates a sequentially coordinated process that begins with metabolic inhibition and cell-cycle regulation, is compounded by 131 I-induced DNA damage with concomitant activation of the cGAS-STING axis, and ultimately translates into enhanced growth suppression and apoptosis, thereby laying the foundation for subsequent in vivo radio-metabolic-immunotherapy.

div.head: Bio-distribution, safety, and antitumor immune activation of 131 I-O/M-P
div.p: Given that 131 I-O/M-P demonstrated clear metabolicimmune modulation and tumoricidal effects at the cellular level, we next evaluated its in vivo bio-distribution, dosing safety, and antitumor/immune-activating activity. Considering the high γ-ray energy of 131 I, and to obtain comparable pharmacokinetic information under identical chemistry while ensuring radiation safety, we first employed 125 I-O/M-P for in vivo tracing. SPECT/CT dynamic imaging revealed visible tumor uptake from 6 h post tail-vein injection (i.v.), reaching a maximum at 24-36 h (Fig. 3A). Concurrently, hepatic uptake was prominent whereas thyroid uptake was negligible, indicating minimal in vivo de-iodination, robust radiochemical stability, and effective accumulation at the tumor site. Ex vivo γ-counting based bio-distribution corroborated the imaging findings: the liver was the major uptake organ, and tumor uptake likewise peaked at 24-36 h, reaching 9.70 ± 2.27%ID/g (Fig. 3B). Subsequent safety assessments (body weight, and hematology/serum biochemistry) showed no evident toxicity (Fig. 3C-E), collectively indicating that 131 I-O/M-P possesses good biocompatibility and in vivo stability, together with strong potential for tumor-targeted delivery.

Having established the in vivo behavior and safety boundaries, we next evaluated the in vivo antitumor efficacy of 131 I-O/M-P and its radiotherapy-associated immune activation. Following treatment, histological analyses were performed on subcutaneous tumors. TUNEL staining revealed more pronounced tumor-cell apoptosis in the 131 I-O/M-P group (Fig. 3F and Fig. S4). In parallel, γ-H2AX signals within tumor tissues were markedly elevated, at least twofold higher than in the O/M-P group (Fig. 3G, H), indicating that 131 I-induced DNA double-strand breaks were effectively amplified in vivo and translated into apoptotic endpoints.

Given that ionizing radiation can generate cytosolic dsDNA fragments and micronuclei that are sensed by cGAS to trigger the STING pathway, we further conducted immunological analyses. Immunofluorescence of tumor tissues showed a clear increase in p-STING after 131 I-O/M-P treatment (Fig. 3I, J), consistent with the aggravated DNA damage described above and indicating activation of the STING axis in vivo. In parallel, flow cytometry revealed that the proportion of mature CD80 + CD86 + DCs in draining lymph nodes increased to 54.46 ± 4.87% (Fig. 3K, L and Fig. S5), and the proportion of macrophages polarized toward the M1 phenotype in tumors (F4/80 + CD86 + ) rose to 41.94 ± 5.33% (Fig. 3M, N and Fig. S6). Taken together, these findings point to two synergistic routes. On the one hand, radiation injury from 131 I activates cGAS-STING via DAMPs and cytosolic DNA, thereby promoting antigen presentation and immune priming. On the other hand, the intrinsic PAMPs and adjuvanticity of OMVs may act in concert with radiation-induced DAMPs to drive DC maturation and macrophage M1 polarization, which helps alleviate the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and amplifies antitumor immunity. As a result, 131 I-O/M-P achieves a chained coupling of radiation damage, innate immune sensing, and adaptive immune activation in vivo.

Hence, 131 I-O/M-P combines good in vivo stability and biocompatibility, clear tumor-targeted accumulation, enhanced radiotoxic killing, and the capacity to remodel the immune microenvironment. By coupling metabolic intervention with radio-sensitization, it amplifies DNA damage; with the adjuvanticity of OMVs and engagement of the STING axis, it promotes DC maturation and M1 macrophage polarization, establishing sequential synergy across the radiation, metabolic and immune dimensions and thereby conferring marked antitumor potential in vivo. ese results provide a rationale and direction for further efficacy assessment in subcutaneous tumor models and for deeper efficacy and expanded immunologic mechanistic studies in orthotopic brain tumor models.

div.head: I-O/M-P mediated radio-metabolic-immunotherapy suppresses glioma progression
div.p: Building on the in vivo behavior and immune activation described above, we next evaluated the comprehensive therapeutic capacity of 131 I-O/M-P in a GL261 subcutaneous tumor model (Fig. 4A). We first assessed overall antitumor efficacy. Compared with O/M-P and 131 I-O-P, 131 I-O/M-P produced the most pronounced tumor suppression, with tumor growth nearly completely abrogated (Fig. 4B and Fig. S7). Histological analyses corroborated these findings. Tumor H&E staining revealed disruption of tissue architecture (Fig. S8), and immunofluorescence for Ki67 and PCNA was markedly reduced (Fig. 4C-F), indicating effective restriction of tumor cell proliferation.

ese therapeutic effects are consistent with the amplified radiation damage and the suppression of replication and repair observed at the cellular and tissue levels, providing a foundation for the subsequent immune-related responses.

On this basis, we assessed markers of ICD to determine their contribution to initiating the antitumor immune cycle. Staining of tumor samples for HMGB1, CRT and HSP70 showed that nuclear HMGB1 signal was diminished in the 131 I-O/M-P group, indicating extracellular release; concomitantly, surface CRT and HSP70 signals were markedly increased (Fig. S9-S11). e ICD induced by 131 I-O/M-P was further validated by quantitative ELISA, which confirmed a significant increase in the extracellular release of HMGB1 and HSP70. ese changes are characteristic of ICD, indicating that the treatment not only imposes strong DNA-damage and apoptotic pressure but also increases the visibility of tumor cells to the immune system, thereby priming subsequent amplification of antitumor responses. Given prior evidence of cGAS-STING activation, DC maturation, and macrophage M1 polarization, we next examined downstream effector cells. Flow-cytometric phenotyping on day 5 after treatment showed that the proportion of intratumoral CD3 + CD8 + Granzyme B + cytotoxic T cells increased to 13.78 ± 0.45% (Fig. 4G, H and Fig. S12), indicating effective mobilization of cytolytic activity. Notably, the fraction of CD3 + CD8 + PD-1 + T cells declined to 1.82 ± 1.39% (Fig. 4I, J and Fig. S13), suggesting that, alongside activation of adaptive immunity, T-cell dysfunction was alleviated, favoring sustained effector function. At the same time, the infiltration of CD45 + NK1.1 + NK cells within tumors rose to 26.20 ± 1.83% (Fig. 4K, L and Fig. S14), implying a parallel enhancement of innate cytotoxicity that complements CTL-mediated killing. To further substantiate these cellular findings, immunofluorescence of tumor sections revealed increased signals for CD3 + CD8 + T cells (Fig. 4M, N) and NK1.1 + cells (Fig. 4O, P), consistent with the flow-cytometric data. Regarding safety, 131 I-O/M-P did not cause significant changes in body weight over the course of treatment (Fig. S15). Post-treatment complete blood counts and serum biochemistry showed no evident abnormalities (Fig. S16), and H&E staining of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney) revealed no discernible differences from controls (Fig. S17), indicating good tolerability and a favorable safety margin at the applied dose and schedule.

Taken together, 131 I-O/M-P achieved radio-metabolicimmunotherapy in the subcutaneous glioma model. On one hand, sustained irradiation from 131 I in combination with MTX-mediated metabolic inhibition synergistically amplified DNA damage while constraining repair, thereby suppressing tumor proliferation. On the other hand, upregulation of ICD markers, activation of the STING axis, maturation of dendritic cells, and polarization of macrophages toward the M1 phenotype promoted effective recruitment and functional maintenance of CTLs and NK cells, further remodeling the immune microenvironment and amplifying antitumor efficacy.
ese results provide a solid basis for validation in orthotopic brain tumor models and for more refined mechanistic studies.

div.head: I-O/M-P suppresses orthotopic glioma and enhances immune modulation
div.p: After confirming the pronounced therapeutic effect of 131 I-O/M-P in subcutaneous tumors, we further evaluated its antitumor efficacy in an orthotopic glioma model. To this end, luciferase-expressing GL261 cells (GL261-Luc) were stereotactically injected into the brains of C57BL/6 mice, and successful tumor establishment was verified 7 days post-implantation by IVIS imaging (Fig. 5A). To characterize in vivo behavior while ensuring radiation safety, we first employed 125 I-O/M-P for tracing. SPECT/CT imaging showed that, following intracranial orthotopic injection, 125 I-O/M-P accumulated stably in the tumor region and maintained high uptake, reaching 71.57 ± 11.99%ID/g at 36 h (Fig. 5B, C). ese indicate favorable local retention and tumor tropism under intracranial administration, providing a pharmacokinetic basis for subsequent efficacy studies.

After defining the bio-distribution profile, we systematically assessed the orthotopic antitumor activity of 131 I-O/M-P (Fig. 5A). IVIS bioluminescence imaging indicated that all mice in the control group died before day 15. Although one mouse still survived in the 131 I-O-P group (G2) on day 20, statistical analysis of the survival curves showed that 131 I-O-P did not produce a significant improvement in survival rates, and the difference was not statistically significant. In contrast, the 131 I-O/M-P group (G3) exhibited marked tumor suppression, with 5 of 6 mice alive on day 20 and complete loss of intracranial bioluminescent signal in 1 of 6 mice. e median survival reached 22.5 days (Fig. 5D, E). ese findings align with the amplified radiation damage and constrained repair observed in vitro and in subcutaneous models, indicating that radio-metabolic synergy can likewise translate into a survival advantage in the intracranial setting. Body weight trajectories supported these outcomes. Unlike the uncontrolled tumor growth in G1, which caused a rapid decline in body weight, and unlike the rapid weight loss in five mice in G2, the 131 I-O/M-P group (G3) showed a transient decrease within 21 days after inoculation that quickly recovered to baseline and even increased (Fig. 5F and Fig. S18). As disease progressed at later time points, however, body weight again declined progressively.

To evaluate histologic tumor control, brains were harvested on day 15-21 after treatment for analysis. Wholebrain H&E sections showed a marked reduction in tumor volume in the 131 I-O/M-P group, with complete tumor disappearance in a subset of mice (Fig. 5G). TUNEL staining indicated prominent apoptosis (Fig. 5H and Fig. S19), and immunofluorescence for Ki67 and PCNA was concurrently and significantly decreased (Fig. 5I, J), consistent with restricted proliferation. GFAP staining was also attenuated (Fig. 5K, L), indicating a reduction in glial-associated markers that may relate to decreased tumor burden and local reactive changes. Notably, MMP-9 expression was suppressed as well (Fig. 5M, N), suggesting reduced invasiveness and angiogenic potential, which aligns with the diminished bioluminescent signal and the extended survival and may reflect secondary remodeling of the tumor microenvironment under conditions of heightened damage and constrained repair.

At the immune level, immune-phenotyping of brain tissues was performed on day 5 after treatment. Compared with controls, both the 131 I-O-P group (G2) and the 131 I-O/M-P group (G3) showed increased proportions of CD3 + CD8 + Granzyme B + cytotoxic T cells (Fig. 5O, P) and CD45 + NK1.1 + NK cells (Fig. 5Q, R), with both populations exceeding 10% in G3. ese findings indicate that 131 I-O/M-P effectively recruits and activates the CTL and NK cytotoxic axes, consistent with the earlier evidence of ICD signaling and STING pathway activation, and they may constitute an immune amplification loop in response to radiation damage. Regarding safety, complete blood counts and serum biochemistry on day 21 showed no obvious abnormalities, and H&E staining of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney) revealed no significant differences from controls (Figs. 5S, T and Fig. S20), indicating good tolerability at the applied dosing regimen.

To sum up, 131 I-O/M-P achieves both radio-sensitization and immune amplification in the orthotopic glioma model. On one hand, sustained β emission from 131 I, in concert with MTX-mediated metabolic intervention, synergistically amplifies DNA damage while constraining repair, directly suppressing tumor growth and conferring a survival benefit. On the other hand, upregulation of ICD markers and activation of the STING pathway promote the recruitment and functional maintenance of CTLs and NK cells, accompanied by M1 polarization and downregulation of MMP-9, which helps reduce invasiveness and remodel the tumor microenvironment.

ese results further demonstrate that 131 I-O/M-P can realize sequential radio-metabolic-immune synergy with marked antitumor potential in the intracranial setting, providing a theoretical basis for metabolism-and immunotherapy-based strategies against brain tumors.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Gliomas are highly invasive central nervous system tumors with pronounced immunosuppression and often develop intrinsic resistance to radiotherapy by enhancing DNA repair and shaping an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In this study, we constructed and systematically validated a multifunctional theranostic platform ( 131 I-O/M-P) that integrates radiotoxic damage, metabolic intervention, and immune activation. Using STATH-engineered OMVs as the carrier, the platform enables efficient, stable labeling with 131 I and high-loading delivery of MTX, while exhibiting favorable physicochemical stability and cellular/in vivo compatibility. In vitro, O/M-P inhibits DHFR and related replication/repair pathways, induces G1/S arrest, and limits DNA synthesis, thereby establishing a pre-emptive "metabolism-replication" weakening prior to irradiation; when combined with 131 I, it markedly amplified γ-H2AX marked DNA damage, enhanced apoptosis, and is accompanied by upregulation of cGAS-STING signaling, demonstrating a clear radio-sensitizing effect. In vivo SPECT/ CT and tissue counting confirmed good tumor accumulation and radiochemical stability of the probe; safety assessments indicated good tolerability at the applied dose and schedule. In GL261 subcutaneous and orthotopic glioma models, 131 I-O/M-P effectively suppressed tumor progression and prolonged survival, with histologic and molecular readouts of decreased proliferation markers (Ki67, PCNA), markedly increased apoptosis, and reduced MMP-9. Immunologic analyses showed that treatment induced ICD (HMGB1 release with upregulation of CRT and HSP70) and activated the STING axis, promoting DC maturation and macrophage M1 polarization, enhancing infiltration of CD8 + Granzyme B + cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, and simultaneously alleviating T-cell exhaustion phenotypes, thereby remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment and establishing a sequential radiation-metabolism-immunity synergy. Overall, with engineered OMVs at its core, 131 I-O/M-P achieves temporal amplification of radiation injury and cascade activation of antitumor immunity, demonstrating substantial potential for brain-tumor therapy and providing a feasible path and theoretical basis for clinical radio-metabolic-immune combination strategies against brain tumors.
